notes: Game 4 of 12 in the experiment, from the Italian Game. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.
result_text: Draw: not enough pieces left to checkmate

This is the Giuoco Piano, and the main central thrust 5.d4 challenges Black's e5 pawn immediately while my c3 pawn supports recapture. After 5...exd4 6.cxd4 Bb4+ 7.Nc3 I get strong central control and fast development; Bxf7+ just loses a piece to Kxf7.

Taking on d4 is the main line of the Giuoco Piano and keeps me from losing a tempo; I checked White's tricks — 6.Bxf7+ Kxf7 7.Qd5+ fails to ...Nxd5 since my f6 knight guards d5, and 6.e5 is met by 6...d5 hitting the bishop. After 6.cxd4 I get ...Bb4+ or ...Bb6 with a healthy game.

This is the main line Giuoco Piano; recapturing with cxd4 builds the ideal pawn centre and opens the c-file, and after 6...Bb4+ I can continue with Bd2 or the sharp Nc3 Greco attack. The alternative 6.e5 d5 allows Black counterplay against my bishop, so I'll take with the pawn.

Bxd4 loses a piece after Nxd4 Nxd4 Qxd4, so the pawn is poisoned; I checked the greedy capture first as my rules demand. Instead I retreat the bishop to b6 where it keeps pressure on the d4/f2 diagonal, stays safe from d4-d5 tempo hits, and if White plays e5 I have ...d5 striking back in the centre.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 7. e5 Ne4 8. Bd5 Ba5+ 9. Kf1 f5

moves.thought: Black's 6...Bb6 leaves the c6-knight loose, so 7.d5 gains central space with tempo — 7...Ne5 just drops a piece to 8.Nxe5, so the knight must retreat to e7 or a5 while my pawn duo and Bc4 dominate. The alternative 7.e5 allows the equalizing 7...d5! 8.exf6 dxc4, so I prefer the space-gaining push.

My c6 knight is attacked by the d5 pawn, and 7...Nxd5 just loses a piece to 8.exd5 (the pawn capture refutes it, per my rule about listing pawn captures). Retreating 7...Ne7 keeps material, maintains the d5 blockade and leaves the e4 knight resource after 8.e5 Ne4.

My e4 pawn is currently undefended and Black threatens Nxe4, so I must either defend it or push; 8.e5 gains a tempo by hitting the f6 knight while keeping the strong d5 wedge, and 8...Nfxd5 fails to 9.Bxd5 Nxd5 10.Qxd5 winning a piece. If Black tries 8...Ne4 I continue 9.d6 cxd6 10.exd6, keeping the initiative and the cramping pawn.

The e5 push hits my f6 knight, and retreats like Nfg8 or Ng4 are passive, so I jump into the centre with Ne4, where no white pawn can capture or chase it (d3 and f3 pawns are gone/weakening) and it eyes f2, d2 and c5. If White plays d6 or Qd3 I reply cxd6 or Nc5 respectively, keeping material level and my pieces defended.

Black's knight on e4 is annoying, but my big pawn duo lets me strike first with 9.d6, undermining the knight on e7: after 9...cxd6 10.exd6 the e7-knight is hit and only Nexd6... actually only the e4-knight can take, after which material is level but Black's pieces are tangled and his king is stuck, letting me pile up with Qe2/O-O/Re1 against the pinned e7-knight. If Black grabs with 9...Nxf2 10.Kxf2 I'm simply a piece up, and 9...Qf6 10.dxe7 wins a knight for a pawn or two.

The d6 pawn attacks my e7 knight, and every "normal" reply (cxd6, Nxd6, or moving the e7 knight) runs into Qd5 hitting my loose e4 knight plus f7, costing material. Ba5+ is a forcing check that makes White stop and block (Nbd2/Bd2/b4/Qd2), after which I can trade off the loose pieces or even snatch b2, and only then solve the e7/c7 problem; against 10.Nc3 I win a rook with Nxc3 bxc3 Bxc3+ Bd2 Bxa1.

The black bishop checks on a5, and I notice the knight on e4 is completely undefended, so blocking with Nbd2 both answers the check and attacks it with tempo. If Black grabs with 10...cxd6 then 11.Nxe4 wins a piece outright, so he's basically forced into 10...Nxd2 11.Bxd2 Bxd2+ 12.Qxd2, after which my cramping d6 pawn and lead in development give me a comfortable initiative.

My knight on e4 has no pawn support and only the loose Nd2 attacks it, while the tempting 10...cxd6 fails to 11.Nxe4 since nothing recaptures on e4. Checking replies, 10...Bxd2+ 11.Qxd2 leaves my unsupported e4 knight short of safe squares (f6 and d6 drop to pawn captures, and ...f5 allows exf6 e.p.) after Qd5, so I simply trade my loosest active piece now; if 11.Bxd2 hits my a5 bishop I answer Bxd2+ and recapture, keeping material level.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 11. Bxd2 Bxd2+ 12. Qxd2 Nc6 13. dxc7 Qxc7

moves.thought: Black is temporarily a piece up, so I must recapture on d2, and Qxd2 is impossible since Bxd2+ would just win my queen on the a5–e1 diagonal. Between Bxd2 and Nxd2 I prefer Bxd2: it keeps my knight on f3 guarding the strong e5/d6 pawn wedge, and after 11...Bxd2+ 12.Qxd2 material is level while Black's knight on e7 and bishop on c8 stay badly cramped.

White's Bd2 attacks my bishop on a5, so I can't grab the d6 pawn yet (11...cxd6 12.Bxa5 wins a piece). Trading the attacked bishop off with check is the cleanest solution: after 11...Bxd2+ 12.Qxd2 I can castle and then pick up the d6 wedge with ...cxd6 or ...Qxc7 recapture, reaching a comfortable game.

Recapturing with the queen is clearly best — Nxd2 or Kxd2 would waste time or cost castling rights, while Qxd2 keeps my development and king safety intact. My advanced d6 and e5 pawns badly cramp Black, whose kingside is undeveloped, and after something like 12...cxd6 13.exd6 I keep a strong passed pawn plus the initiative.

The d6 pawn is annoying but it's also loose and White's pieces aren't yet coordinated, so I prioritise king safety and connecting rooks rather than committing to 12...cxd6 13.exd6 when my knight gets chased and my c8 bishop stays dead. After 12...0-0, White's best is 13.dxc7 Qxc7 (developing my queen with pressure on e5) or 13.d7 Bxd7, both fine for me; I checked 13.Bxf7+ Rxf7 and 13.e6 fxe6 14.Bxe6+ dxe6 just lose material for White, and Ne7 still covers d5 against Qd5 tricks.

review.label: mistake
review.refutation: 13. dxe7 Qxe7 14. O-O d6 15. exd6 Qxd6

moves.thought: The knight on e7 has been hanging to my d6 pawn ever since 9.d6, and Black never resolved it — c7xd6 was the needed defense but Black castled instead. Taking with dxe7 simply wins a knight for a pawn after Qxe7, and my e5 pawn stays protected by Nf3 so there's no counter-tactic like Qxe5+.

The e7 pawn attacks both my queen and f8 rook, so I must eliminate it; I checked every white piece (Bc4, Nf3, Qd2, rooks, king) and none of them covers e7, so Qxe7 simply regains the pawn for free. Follow-ups like Bxf7+ Rxf7 or Qd5 achieve nothing since f7 stays defended by king and rook, and my queen on e7 is attacked by nothing.

I'm up a full knight for a pawn, so my main jobs are to hold the e5 pawn (Black threatens Qxe5+) and keep the king safe. Qd4 defends e5, centralizes, and conveniently covers b4 so there's no annoying ...Qb4+ check; if Black hits the queen with ...c5 I can retreat to c3 still guarding e5 and b4, then castle and trade down into a winning endgame.

I'm a piece down, so I first screened every queen move for pawn/piece capturers: Qxe5+ Nxe5, Qd6/Qf6 exd6-exf6, Qg5/Qh4 Nx, Qa3 bxa3, Qc5 Qxc5 and Qe6 Bxe6 all drop the queen, and ...d5/...b5 just lose a pawn to the c4 bishop. The solid choice is 14...d6, which is doubly defended (Qe7 and c7), challenges the cramping e5 pawn and finally frees my c8 bishop; after 15.exd6 cxd6 or 15.Qxd6 Qxd6 16.exd6 cxd6 nothing more is lost.

I'm up a knight for a pawn, so simplification favors me — Qxd6 grabs the weak d-pawn and offers a queen trade on e7's diagonal. If Black answers ...Qxe5+ then Nxe5 just wins the queen, and after ...Qxd6 exd6 cxd6 I reach a trivially winning endgame a piece ahead.

White's 15.Qxd6 ignored that my c7 pawn also guards d6, so 15...cxd6 simply wins the queen; after 16.exd6 Qxd6 the recapture pawn is undefended (Bc4 and Nf3 don't cover d6) and I come out queen for knight ahead. The passive 15...Qxd6 16.exd6 cxd6 would instead leave me a knight down, so I take with the pawn.

I'm down a queen for a knight after the earlier Qxd6 blunder, so my priority is king safety and a solid structure rather than more material loss — Bxf7+ and e6 just drop material since Black recaptures favourably. Castling kingside tucks the king away, connects the rooks, and keeps e5 safely defended by Nf3 (Qxe5 would lose the queen to Nxe5).

I'm a queen for a knight up, so I just need safe consolidation — and I noticed Qxe5 would be a disaster because Nf3 guards e5 (Qxe5 Nxe5 loses the queen). Instead dxe5 wins the pawn cleanly since my queen on e7 defends e5, so Nxe5 simply drops the knight to Qxe5, and Bxf7+ is answered by Rxf7 or Kh8 with nothing for White.

I'm down heavy material (queen for bishop and knight plus a pawn), so I need maximum activity rather than desperate sacrifices — Bxf7+ Kxf7 Nxe5+ only trades my good bishop for two pawns and worsens the balance. Instead Rae1 piles up on the loose e5 pawn (Nf3 and Re1 against the queen's lone defence), keeps my strong bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal, and develops with tempo; if Black answers Qc5 I simply retreat the bishop to d5 or b3.

My e5 pawn is attacked twice (Nf3, Re1) and defended only by my queen, so Nxe5 Qxe5 Rxe5 would win my queen — exactly the stacked-attackers trap from rules 1 and 2. Pushing e4 solves it with tempo: nothing can capture e4 (the knight on f3 doesn't cover it, Rxe4 just loses a rook to Qxe4) and the pawn simultaneously kicks the knight, after which ...Bf5 will give the pawn a second defender if needed, keeping my queen-for-two-pieces edge.

I'm down a queen for a knight after the earlier blunder, so I need to regain material and keep my pieces safe; the e4 pawn is attacked by Re1 but defended by the queen on e7. Captures like Bxf7+ just drop a piece (f7 is triply defended), and Nd4/Ne5/Ng5 all run into ...Qc5 forking my loose bishop and knight, whereas Nd2 adds a second attacker on e4 without creating a fork target.

White threatens Nxe4 (knight and rook hit the pawn), and I checked that Bc4 is actually defended by Nd2, so 18...Qc5 is refuted by 19.b4 gaining tempo, while 18...Rd8 19.Nxe4 Rd4 runs into 20.Nf6+! gxf6 21.Rxe7 trading my queen off. 18...Bf5 develops my last piece, defends e4, and every capture (Nxe4 Bxe4 Rxe4, or Rxe4 Bxe4 Nxe4) leaves me comfortably up queen-for-knight with no loose pieces or weakened king.

I'm down heavy material (queen for a bishop earlier), so I need activity rather than trades that liquidate my minor pieces; Nxe4 and Rxe4 both just drop material to Bxe4, and f3 loses the bishop to Qc5+. Bd5 is safe, adds a third attacker to e4, and immediately threatens Bxb7 as well as pressure on f7.

I'm up a queen for a knight, so I just need to consolidate: e4 is hit three times (Bd5, Nd2, Re1) and only defended by Bf5, so Rfe8 adds a defender behind which my Qe7 also bears down the e-file — the whole sequence Nxe4 Bxe4 Bxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 Qxe4 nets me a knight. Keeping the a8 rook home also guards b7 against Bxb7, and Bxf7+ simply loses a bishop to Kxf7.

I'm down a queen for two pieces, so I need to grab material and simplify where I can; capturing e4 loses out because Black's queen and rook outnumber my pieces on the e-file (Bxe4 Bxe4 Nxe4 Rxe4! Rxe4 Qxe4). Instead Bxb7 snatches a pawn and hits the a8 rook, and if Black counters with e3 or Qb4 I simply take on a8 with a winning material swing.

White's bishop just took on b7 and is completely undefended — the knight on d2 and both rooks cannot reach b7, and my queen's path along the 7th rank (d7, c7) is clear. After Qxb7 the only tactic is Nxe4, but my bishop on f5 guards it (Nxe4 Bxe4 Rxe4 Qxe4), so I simply win a piece and stay a queen-plus up.

Material is level, but Black's advanced e4 pawn is his only weakness — it's attacked twice (Re1, Nd2) and defended twice (Bf5, Re8), so capturing now loses material (Rxe4 Bxe4 Nxe4 Rxe4). Instead I add a third attacker by lining up on the e-file with Re3, intending Rfe1 (and possibly f3), after which Nxe4 Bxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 nets me the pawn; 21...Bg4 would even lose the pawn immediately to Nxe4.

I checked that b2 is captured by no pawn (a2 only captures to b3) and no piece guards it, and from b2 my queen also hits the completely loose Nd2 along the second rank, so Qxb2 wins a pawn with a threat; meanwhile e4 stays adequately defended since Nxe4 Bxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 and Rxe4 Rxe4 Nxe4 Bxe4 are both even trades that only help me with a queen for a knight extra.

My knight on d2 is hanging to Qxd2, so I must address it — and Nb3 is the best way: the knight gets protected by the a2 pawn, covers d4 (so Qd4 would just be met by Nxd4), and heads for d4 where it hits the bishop on f5. Nc4 fails to Qd4 forking knight and rook, while Nf3 drops a piece to exf3; I accept losing the a2 pawn in return for activity.

I first checked the captures: Qxb3 loses the queen to axb3 and Qxf2+ loses it to Rxf2, while Qd4 drops the queen to Nxd4 since the knight covers that square — exactly the pawn/piece-defender trap my notebook warns about. Qxa2 is completely safe (b3's knight does not cover a2, and my e4 pawn stays guarded by Bf5 and Re8), it wins a pawn, and it leaves the b3 knight undefended so Ra1 would just run into Qxb3.

I'm down a huge amount of material, and worse, my knight on b3 is hanging to the queen on a2, so I must move it. Nd4 saves the knight on a safe square while attacking the bishop on f5, which is the only defender of the e4 pawn, so I may win that pawn back next move.

My bishop on f5 is attacked by Nd4 while the e4 pawn hangs to Re3, so I need one move that solves both; Bg6 retreats the bishop to a square no knight, rook or pawn can reach while still guarding e4 along the g6-b1 diagonal. White's tries (Nf5, Ne6, Nc6, Rxe4) all just lose material to Bxf5, fxe6, Rxe3 or Bxe4, so I keep my overwhelming queen-plus-material edge with the simplest consolidating move.

I'm down a lot of material, so I need to keep pieces active and avoid loose ones; Rxe4 just drops a rook to Bxe4 since the g6 bishop guards it. Rfe1 doubles on the e-file, keeps e3 protected (f2 plus the rook), doubles the attack on the e4 pawn, and if Black hits my knight with ...Qd2 I have Nb3 to kick the queen back.

I'm up a queen and bishop for a knight, so I just need safe consolidation: my e4 pawn is attacked twice by the rooks but defended by Re8 and Bg6, and any Rxe4 sequence costs White two rooks for a rook and pawn. Qd5 centralises safely (no white pawn or piece covers d5, and Nd4 doesn't attack it), adds a third defender to e4, and attacks the completely undefended knight on d4 — Nb5/Nc6 drop it to my queen, and Nf5 drops it to Bxf5.

My knight on d4 is hanging to the queen, so I must move it, and I need to keep my two rooks coordinated since I'm down material and need maximum solidity. Ne2 retreats the knight to a square guarded twice by my rooks, keeps the e-file blocked, and prepares Nc3 to hit both the e4 pawn and the queen; captures like Rxe4 fail because after Rxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 Qxe4 I simply lose a rook.

I'm up a queen and bishop for a knight, so I only need safety: I checked the knight on e2's attack squares (c1, c3, d4, f4, g3, g1) and rejected Qd4 because Nxd4 simply takes my queen, and Qd1 because Rxd1 does the same. Re5 is defended by my queen, is immune to the e-file rooks since my own e4 pawn blocks them, and if White ever takes on e4 the sequence Rxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 Bxe4 nets me two rooks for a bishop and a pawn.

I'm hopelessly down material, so I need the most forcing practical try: Nf4 is safe (nothing on d5, e5, g6 or g7 can capture it) and forks the queen on d5 and the bishop on g6. If Black grabs with Qd4 or Qd2 I defend or take the bishop on g6, and only Qd6 holds everything together.

My queen is attacked by Nf4, so I must move it, and I want a square that keeps my e4 pawn defended against Re3 while staying safe from pawns and pieces — Qd4 does both and also hits the undefended-by-pawn rook on e3. I checked White's replies: Rxe4 loses a rook to Rxe4/Qxe4, Nd3 drops the knight to Qxd3, and Nxg6 is simply met by hxg6, so I keep my overwhelming queen-and-bishop-for-knight material edge with no loose pieces.

I'm down a queen for a knight, so my main hope is simplification and solidity: Re3 is attacked by Qd4 but defended by Re1, and Rxe4 fails since e4 is defended three times (Rxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 Qxe4 just drops two rooks). Nxg6 is a clean equal trade that eliminates Black's active bishop, which controls d3/f5/e4 and supports the e4 pawn, without weakening my e-file blockade.

White's knight just took my bishop on g6 and is also attacking my rook on e5, so I must recapture at once rather than add defenders. I prefer hxg6 over fxg6 because it keeps the f7 pawn guarding my king's back rank and the g6 pawn covers f5/h5; after hxg6 White's pressure on e4 is answered by Re5/Qd4 (Rxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 Qxe4 loses two rooks for one), leaving me a clean queen plus two pawns ahead.

Black's main resource is the liquidating ...Qxe3, so I need to get my rook off e3 while keeping both rooks mutually defended and the e-file blocked. R3e2 doubles the rooks, protects e1 (so ...Qd2 ideas fail to Rxe2 trading queen for rook), and keeps the e4 pawn under restraint; taking on e4 fails since Rxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 Qxe4 just drops both rooks.

I'm a whole queen and two pawns up, so I just need to consolidate: the e4 pawn blocks White's rooks and is already covered twice (rook first, then queen, so Rxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 Qxe4 wins two rooks for a rook and pawn). Rae8 brings my last piece in and adds a third e-file unit, while I avoid 28...Qxf2+ (voluntarily trading queen for rook) and 28...e3, which after fxe3 Rxe3 Rxe3 leaves my queen unable to recapture safely because Re1 guards e3.

Black is threatening 29...Rxe2 30.Rxe2 Rxe2 winning a whole rook, since my king can't recapture on e2, and 29.Rxe4 Rxe4 30.Rxe4 Qxe4 leaves me with nothing against queen and four pawns. By playing Re3 I keep the rooks doubled behind the e4 pawn, which itself blocks the file so Black's rooks can never come to e3, and 29...Qxe3 just loses the queen to Rxe3.

I rejected Qxe3 since it voluntarily gives queen for rook (rule 11) and only nets back a pawn after fxe3 Rxe3 Rxe3. Instead Qd2 is untouchable (no pawn or piece covers d2), hits f2, and sets up the real threat ...Qxe1+ Rxe1 Rxe1 mate, forcing White to weaken further while I keep my queen and extra material.

I'm down a queen for a rook, so my only practical hope is activity and repetition — Rxe4 just trades into a hopeless king-and-pawns endgame against queen and rook. R3e2 hits the queen with tempo, keeps f2 and e4 under control, and invites the same Re3/Qd2 cycle we just had, which could give me a repetition draw if Black isn't careful.

I'm a whole queen up, so the key is to avoid the tempting Qxe1+/Qxe2, which just swap my queen for a rook against a doubled, defended rook pair (my notebook rule 11). Qd4 centralizes safely, adds a defender to the e4 pawn (so Rxe4 Rxe4 Rxe4 Qxe4 wins both rooks for me), and White has no checks or captures that touch my pieces.

I'm down a queen, and my rooks are tied to the e-file — Re1 must stay to defend Re2, since any rook move off the file (Rd1, Rc2, etc.) drops material to Qxe2 or Rxe1+, and Rxe4 or Re3 just liquidates into a lost queen-versus-rook ending. Black's plan is e3, so I'll make a luft with h3 and keep the defensive setup intact as long as possible.

I'm up a queen for nothing, so my priority is to avoid the rank-2/rank-1 queen traps (Qd2, Qb2, Qa1, Qd1 all drop the queen to Rxd2/Rxa1/Rxd1) and to avoid the greedy Qxf2+ Kxf2 line that voluntarily swaps queen for rook. Pushing e3 is safe: it's defended by Qd4 and Re5, and after 32.fxe3 Rxe3 33.Rxe3 Rxe3 34.Rxe3 Qxe3+ every rook comes off leaving me a queen and four pawns against two pawns, while 32.f4 simply loses a rook to 32...Rxe2 33.Rxe2 Qd1+.

I'm hopelessly behind on material, so my best practical chance is to liquidate as many pieces as possible: 32.Rxe3 forces exchanges on e3 (if 32...Qxe3 33.Rxe3 Rxe3 34.fxe3 I even trade the queen off into a rook endgame), whereas quiet moves like f3 or f4 let Black push e2 and keep all the attackers.

White's rook on e3 is attacked three times (Re5, Re8 behind it, and Qd4) but defended only once by Re1, so counting the full sequence: Rxe3 Rxe3 Rxe3 leaves me a whole rook up with White having no heavy pieces left. The e8 rook is blocked by my e5 rook, so Rxe3 must be the e5 rook, and nothing is left loose afterwards.

I'm down a queen for a rook, so my only practical course is to liquidate pieces: Rxe3 forces matters, since Qxe3 would lose the queen to fxe3, so Black must reply Rxe3 and after fxe3 Qxe3+ a pair of rooks is off the board. Keeping the rook with moves like Re2 or Rf1 just loses it for nothing to Rxe2 or Qxe1+, so the trade is the least bad.

I'm up a queen for nothing, and e3 is attacked twice (Re8 and Qd4) but defended only by the f2 pawn, so Rxe3 fxe3 Qxe3+ wins the rook and the pawn, leaving queen and four pawns against three pawns — a trivially won ending. This simplifies rather than inventing anything clever, and nothing of mine is left loose.

I'm down a queen for nothing, so my only practical try is to grab the rook with fxe3, cutting the material deficit to just queen versus two pawns. Black will reply Qxe3+ and I'll tuck the king on h2, hoping for a long technical conversion where something might go wrong.

I'm a whole queen up against a bare king with three pawns, so the simplest route is to grab the e3 pawn with check and then pick off g2/h3 or escort my own pawns home. After Qxe3+ Kh2 (or Kf1/Kh1) there are no counter-threats whatsoever.

I'm down a queen for nothing after the rook trades, so I just need the safest king square; Kh1 risks getting boxed in the corner, while Kh2 keeps my king near g2 and off the long diagonal/back rank. I'll play Kh2 and try to hold on.

Qxh3+ is the trap my rule 5 warns about — the g2 pawn simply recaptures and I lose my queen for a pawn. Instead I check with Qf4+ to drive the white king into the corner, keeping all my pawns safe, after which I can bring my own king up and mate with queen against two pawns.

I'm down a queen for nothing, so I just need the most resilient king move; g3 loses the g-pawn immediately to Qxg3+ followed by Qxh3+. Kg1 keeps my king off the edge and avoids back-rank/corner mating nets better than Kh1.

I'm a whole queen up against a bare king with only g2/h3 pawns, so per rule 8 I just need the simplest consolidating plan: march my king up the h-file (Kh7–h6–h5) to help the queen force mate, while the queen on f4 already covers the kingside and stops any g4/h4 counterplay. No captures or checks by White are available, and nothing is loose, so Kh7 is completely safe and avoids any stalemate tricks like grabbing g2 undefended.

I'm a queen down in a lost endgame, so my only aim is to avoid giving away free pawns. g3, g4 and h4 all drop a pawn immediately to the queen on f4, while Kh1 keeps g2 defended by the king and nothing is capturable.

I'm a queen for two pawns up with White's king cornered on h1, so I just need a safe, forcing plan: Qf2 takes g1, g2 and h2 away from the king, leaving White only pawn pushes while I march my king up via h6-g5 to help mate. I'll keep the stalemate risk in mind and simply step the queen aside if White ever runs out of pawn moves.

Black threatens Qf1+ followed by Qxg2#, so g4 and h4 lose on the spot; I must address the back-rank mating net. Kh2 keeps the g2 pawn defended by the king (so Qxg2 is impossible) and gives my king the g1/h1 squares to shuffle between, which is the toughest defence in this lost ending.

I have queen plus four pawns against two pawns, so I only need a safe, non-losing move — crucially Qxg2+, Qg3+ and Qg1+ all drop the queen to the king on h2 since those squares are undefended. Qf4+ is completely out of reach of White's king and pawns, drives the king to the back rank, and lets me bring my king up afterwards.
I'm a queen down, so my only hope is to avoid immediate mate and keep shuffling. g3 loses to Qxg3+ Kh1 Qg2#, and Kh1 allows Qf1+ Kh2 Qxg2#; Kg1 is safe because Qf1+ there would simply be met by Kxf1.

I'm a whole queen up against a bare king with only g2/h3 pawns, so the simplest winning plan is to keep the queen on f4 (covering h2 and the g3 square) and walk my king in via h6-g5-f4 to deliver mate, while watching out for any stalemate tricks. Kh6 is completely safe since White has no checks, captures, or threats at all.

I'm hopelessly down a queen, so my only practical hopes are the 50-move rule or a stalemate trick, which means I should avoid pawn moves that reset the counter and hand Black free targets (g3 and h4 just drop a pawn, g4 weakens further). Kh1 keeps my pawn structure intact and keeps the halfmove clock ticking while Black has to find the mating technique.

I'm a queen and three pawns up versus two bare pawns, so my only tasks are to avoid stalemate tricks and never trade the queen for the g2/h3 pawns (h3 is guarded by g2). Qf3 centralises safely, covers g3/g4/h3 so White's pawns can't come out with tempo, and prepares my king's march via g5 to h4 while always leaving White a legal king move.

Black's queen just stepped onto f3 where my g2 pawn can simply capture it — the pawn isn't pinned since the g2 pawn itself blocks the f3-h1 diagonal, so there's no check. Winning the queen for a pawn transforms a hopeless position into a mere pawn endgame.

With queens gone I'm two pawns up in a pure pawn race, so I counted it: my a-pawn needs five moves (a5-a4-a3-a2-a1) while White's king on h1 needs six tempi just to reach b1/b2, so it can never enter the square of the passer. If White tries h4-h5 for counterplay I simply answer gxh5 (or Kh5) and keep both my passer and my f/g majority.

I'm down to two pawns against four and Black's outside a-pawn is faster than my king, so I have to start the king march immediately and hope for a blockade. Kg2 heads for the queenside via f2-e3-d4, which is my only practical try; h4 or f4 just weaken my own pawns without slowing the a-pawn.

I'm a clean pawn up with a far-advanced passed a-pawn, and White's king on g2 is well outside the square (a5-a1-e1-e5), so the race is winning: a4-a3-a2-a1 promotes in four moves while White's king needs six to reach the corner. White's f3/h3 pawns are nowhere near promoting and my king on h6 covers that wing, so the race is one-sided.

I'm two pawns down and Black's a-pawn is running: after 43.Kf2 a3 44.Ke2 a2 45.Kd2 a1=Q my king can't arrive in time, but it's my only practical try since my f- and h-pawns can't create a passer against f7/g7/g6 with the black king nearby. Pushing f4 or h4 just loses a pawn and a tempo, so I'll head toward the queenside.

My a-pawn is already outside the square of White's king (square a4–a1–d1–d4, king on f2), so it promotes in three moves while White's f3/h3 pawns need five to do anything; a3 a2 a1=Q wins by force with no stalemate or counter-race risk.

Black's a-pawn will queen unless I run for it, so my only practical try is the king race: 44. Ke2 a2 45. Kd2 Kc2 Kb2 and Kxa2. Keeping the h3 pawn as a speed bump, Ke2 is the fastest route toward the corner, one tempo quicker than any kingside move.

My a-pawn on a3 is a passer and White's king on e2 is too far to control a1 — after 44...a2 nothing can stop 45...a1=Q next move, since the king needs three moves (d2-c2-b2) to reach a1's guard. I checked White has no checks or counter-threats, and my king on h6 is safe behind f7/g7/g6, so promoting is the simplest win.

Black's a-pawn is unstoppable — my king on e2 is too far to catch it, so promotion is coming regardless. I choose Kd2 because it brings my king closest to the corner while keeping c1/c2 covered, so the new queen appears without check (unlike Kd1, where a1=Q is check and gains a tempo), giving me the best chance to harass it while my f/h pawns stay mobile.

My a2 pawn promotes immediately and the white king on d2 cannot reach a1, so I simply get a new queen against a bare king with two loose pawns. Queen plus three pawns versus two pawns is a trivially won ending, and nothing in the position allows White any counterplay or stalemate trick.

I'm down a queen for nothing, so my only practical hope is to keep my king active and my pawns defended while making Black work for the win. Ke3 centralizes, shields the f3 pawn, and keeps the king off the a1-h8 and first-rank lines where the new queen is strongest, even if Black can harass with checks.

I'm a whole queen up, so the only real danger is giving the queen away — and indeed Qd4+ would be met by Kxd4 since d4 touches the white king and is undefended, so I rule it out. Qe5+ is a safe centralising check (e5 is not adjacent to e3 and cannot be captured) that drives the king back and lets me follow up by bringing my king forward to mate.

I'm down a queen for two pawns, so my only hope is to keep my king active and run it away from Black's king on h6. Kd3 is safe (d3 isn't covered by the queen on e5), keeps the king central with the most escape squares, and heads toward the open queenside, whereas Kf2 lets the queen check from e3/e2 and drive me back while Black's king approaches my pawns.

I'm a queen and a pawn up with no counterplay to fear, so I want a simple forcing move that gains material safely: Qe4+ is check from an untouchable square and simultaneously attacks the loose f3 pawn, and none of White's king retreats (Kd2, Kc3, Kc2) defend it. After winning f3 and then h3 my king can walk up with the queen covering every approach square, which is far cleaner than rushing my own pawns.

The new queen on e4 is completely undefended — Black's king sits on h6 and no pawn covers e4 — so I simply capture it. I prefer Kxe4 over fxe4 because it leaves my king superbly centralised, and Black's extra pawn is a doubled g-pawn, which gives me real drawing chances in the resulting 2-v-3 same-side pawn ending.

The key square is f4 — if I let the white king settle there it blockades everything, so I grab g5 first with my king, denying f4/g4 and preparing both ...f5 and ...Kh4 to win the h3 pawn. The only forcing try 49.f4+ fails to 49...Kg4!, when h3 is undefended and I keep three pawns against one with my king in front of White's passer; after quieter 49.Ke3 I continue ...f5 and ...Kh4 with my extra pawn intact.

My h3 pawn is doomed to ...Kh4, so my only resource is a king raid: Kd5–e6 hits f7, and after ...Kxh3 Kxf7 the g-pawns (doubled, undefended once f7 falls) drop too — e.g. 49.Kd5 Kg4 50.Ke6 Kxf3 51.Kxf7 Kg3 52.Kxg6 Kxh3 53.Kxg7 is a dead draw. I prefer Kd5 over Ke5 because it avoids the tempo-gaining ...f6+ while reaching e6 just as quickly.

My king on g5 can step to f4 attacking the undefended f3 pawn, and White's king on d5 cannot reach e4/e5 to defend it, so after 50.Kd4 Kxf3 I am two clean pawns up with my king also within easy reach of the lone h-pawn (Kg4 stops any h4-h5 run). That gives a trivially winning king-and-pawns ending rather than letting White's king come back toward my pawns.

My f3 pawn is attacked and no king move can defend it, so I'm losing material either way. Playing h4 at least creates a trading chance: if Black answers g5, hxg5 Kxg5 trades a pair and leaves me one pawn against two instead of facing three. Otherwise after Kxf3 I'd still be lost, so h4 offers the best practical hope.

White's f3 pawn is undefended, so Kxf3 leaves me three pawns (f7/g6/g7) against the lone h4 pawn, and if White tries Ke5 then Kg4 also picks up h4 while my king stays beside my pawn mass. I checked the king raid Ke6 Kxf7: I answer with ...g5 and ...f6 so my own passer runs with White's king stuck behind it, so no pawn race catches me out.

I'm three pawns down, so my only hope is to activate my king and eat the kingside pawns while Black's king is far on f3. After 51.Ke5 Kg4 52.Kf6 Kxh4 53.Kxf7 Kg5 54.Kxg7 I reach a drawn K+P vs K with my king in front of the g6 pawn; pushing h5 instead just gives Black a passed h-pawn.

White's king is desperate to reach f6, where it would hit f7, g7 and g6 all at once, so I take that square away with check and gain a tempo — now g7 defends f6 and White's only route in is via f7. After 52.Ke6 Kg4 53.Kf7 I play Kh5! (not Kxh4, which allows Kxg6 picking up everything), keeping g6 guarded; then ...Kg5 holds f6 and g6 while my f-pawn runs, and White's king can never both blockade g6 and catch it.

I'm in check from the f6 pawn and must move my king; I'm hopelessly down material, so I want the most active square. Ke6 keeps my king pressing against the f6/g6/g7 pawn mass and gives Black the most chance to go wrong, whereas retreating with Kd4/Kd5/Kd6 abandons them entirely.

My f6 pawn is only safe because g7 guards it, so I must not break the chain yet — 52...g5 53.hxg5 fxg5 54.Kf5 wins my g5 pawn and 52...Kg4 53.Kxf6 Kxh4 54.Kxg6 liquidates into a draw. Instead I centralise with Kf4, which keeps every pawn defended and prepares ...g5 with king support: after 53.Kf7 g5 54.hxg5 fxg5 55.Kxg7 g4 my king escorts the pawn home while White's king is outside the square.

Down to a single h-pawn against three, I need activity: Kf7 attacks g7 and forces liquidation. After 53...g5 54.hxg5 fxg5 55.Kxg7, or 53...Kg4 54.Kxg7 Kxh4 55.Kxf6, I end up with my king in front of Black's last pawn, which should hold the draw; by contrast 53.h5 gxh5 just leaves me pawnless against two runners and losing.

White's king on f7 is about to munch g6/g7, so I must create a runner now: 53...g5! After 54.hxg5 fxg5 55.Kxg7 my king on f4 escorts the g-pawn while White's king is stuck behind it (...g4, g3, g2, g1 promotes with the king too far to reach the g-file), and 54.Kxg7 gxh4 is the same race won easily.

Kxg7 loses because 54...gxh4 leaves Black a free runner my king can't catch, and 54. h5 g4 55. h6 gxh6! gives Black three pawns against nothing. Taking with 54. hxg5 liquidates: after fxg5 (or Kxg5) I grab the g7 pawn and my king sits directly in front of the lone g-pawn on the fifth rank, which is a textbook draw.

fxg5 wins White's last pawn and keeps a passed g-pawn that my king on f4 already defends; even after 55.Kxg7, ...g4 runs home because White's king on g7 is six moves from g1 while the pawn needs only three (56.Kg6 g3 57.Kg5 g2 58.Kg4 g1=Q). Kxg5 also wins but leaves only the slower f6 pawn after Kxg7, and ...g6 would be a blunder since gxf6 gives White a passer that promotes first.

I'm a pawn down with no pawns of my own, so my only hope is to eliminate material and get my king in front of the last pawn; Kxg7 removes one pawn and leaves K+P vs K where any black king move (like Kg4) lets me take the drawing square with Kg6. Pushing lines like 55...g4 56.Kxg7 g3 would still be lost for me, but grabbing the g7 pawn gives the best practical drawing chances.

White's king on g7 is behind my pawn, so it must detour via the h- or f-file to reach the stopping squares g3/g2/g1 — it can't get there in time. After 55...g4 (defended by Kf4) I calculated 56.Kg6 Kf3 57.Kg5 g3 (58.Kg4 is illegal, the kings touch) g2 and 59.Kh3 g1=Q, and the same race wins after 56.Kh6 Kf3 57.Kh5 g3 58.Kh4 g2 59.Kh3 g1=Q, so this is a won K+P ending with my king in front of the pawn.

The g-pawn is outside my king's square (three moves to queen, six for my king to reach g1), so I can't stop it; my only practical try is to keep my king as close as possible and hope for a stalemate trick after promotion. Kf6 heads toward the pawn and the enemy king fastest.

I checked the square rule: after 56...g3 the pawn needs only two more moves (g2, g1) while White's king on f6 needs at least five to reach g1/g2, so it is far outside the square and cannot catch the pawn or be helped by my own king blocking f4. Candidates Kg3/Kf3 also win but are slower and let the white king approach; 56...g3 promotes by force into a trivially winning K+Q vs K.

I can't catch the g-pawn — my king on f6 is five moves from g1 while the pawn needs only two — so queening is unavoidable. I'll keep my king as close to the pawn and the new queen as possible with Kg6, hoping for a stalemate or perpetual-check-style resource rather than drifting away with Ke7/Kf7.

My g-pawn is one step from promotion and White's king on g6 needs four moves to reach g1/g2, so it cannot stop it; after 57...g2 58.any g1=Q I have a trivially winning king-and-queen vs king ending. I checked that White has no check, capture or blockade available, and my king on f4 stays close enough to escort the new queen to mate.

My king on g6 is far too distant to catch the g2 pawn, so Black promotes next move and I'm lost regardless; there's no stalemate resource available. I'll play Kf6 to keep my king centralized and near Black's king, giving the best practical chance of a mistake or perpetual-avoidance.
I just promote to a queen — king and queen versus a bare king is a trivial, known win, and I checked it is not stalemate since White's king still has e6, e7 and f7 available after g1=Q.

I'm hopelessly lost down a queen with a bare king, so I just try to stay off the edge and away from a quick mating net. Ke6 keeps my king as central as possible; I checked that none of Qg6+, Qe1+ or anything else mates immediately, whereas drifting to the back ranks with Ke7/Kf7 invites a faster mate.

This is a basic king-and-queen mate, so I use the knight's-distance technique: Qg7 sits a knight's move from the white king and, together with my king covering e5/f5/g5, cuts his available squares down to just d5 and d6 without any stalemate risk. The queen is far from the white king, so it can never be attacked while I walk my king in.

I'm down to a bare king against queen and king, so the game is lost; I just want to avoid immediate mate and stay off the edge while keeping distance from the black king. Kd6 moves away from the black king on f4, and the natural Qd7+ there would just lose the queen to my king, so it's the most stubborn try.

With queen versus bare king I just need safe confinement, so I avoid the tempting checks Qc7+/Qd7+/Qe7+ that simply lose the queen to Kx, and instead play the knight's-distance move Qf7, which is untouchable and shrinks White's king to c5/c6 (e5/e6/d5/d7/e7 all covered or adjacent to my king). Then I walk my king over with Ke3/Ke4 and mate.

I'm down to a bare king against queen and king, so the game is lost; neither move changes that. Kc6 keeps my king off the edge and a bit further from Black's king on f4, so I'll play that and make Black work for the mate.

I first checked the tempting adjacent checks — Qd7+, Qb7+, Qc7+ and Qd5+ all put my undefended queen next to the white king, so Kxd7/Kxb7/Kxc7/Kxd5 simply takes it. Qe7 keeps the queen a knight's move from c6 (untouchable), cuts the 7th rank and e-file, confining White to b5/b6/c5/d5/d6 while my king walks over to help mate.

I'm a lone king against queen and king, so the game is lost; I just need to avoid the fastest mate and keep away from the edge as long as possible. Kd5 invites Qd7+ pinning me to the rim, and Kb6 lets the queen cut me off quickly, so I'll step to b5 to keep maximum room.

With queen and king versus a bare king I just need to shrink the white king's box without ever putting my undefended queen next to it (so Qb4+/Qc5+ are out, as Kxb4/Kxc5 draws). Qd6 is a knight's-move away from b5, covers the whole 6th rank, the d-file and the b4/c5 diagonal, leaving White only a4, a5 or c4 while my king starts marching over.

I'm down to a bare king against queen and king, so my only practical hopes are stalemate tricks or a blunder; Ka4 or Ka5 push me toward the edge where the mating net closes fastest. Kc4 keeps my king central with the maximum number of flight squares and even baits Qd4+, which I could simply capture since Black's king on f4 doesn't guard that square.

This is a basic K+Q vs K mate, and my queen on d6 already sits a knight's move from the white king, boxing it into the a1–c5 corner; so the correct plan is simply to march my king up rather than give a check on an adjacent square (Qb4+, Qc5+, Qd4+, Qd3+, Qd5+ all lose the queen to Kx). Ke4 brings my king closer with no stalemate risk, since White still has b3, b4, b5 and c3.

I'm down to a bare king against a queen, so I just need to stay off the edge and avoid immediate mate while hoping for a stalemate or the 50-move rule. Kc3 keeps my king centralized, and I checked that no queen move (Qb4+, Qc5+, Qd3+) delivers mate next move since squares like b2 and d2 stay free.

With king and queen versus a bare king, I use the knight-move restriction technique: Qd5 sits a knight's leap from White's king on c3, is protected by my king on e4, and confines White to a tiny box (only b2, b4, c2 are available) with no stalemate risk. From there I shrink the box with further knight-move queen placements and walk my king over to deliver mate on the edge.

I'm hopelessly lost with a bare king against queen and king, so I just want to stay off the edge and avoid walking into an immediate check. Kb4 allows Qa5+ driving me back, and Kb2 heads toward the corner, whereas Kc2 keeps my king as central as possible (and Qd2+ there would simply lose the queen to Kxd2).

With K+Q vs lone king I just need to box White in safely, and the key check Qd3+ is protected by my king on e4 so Kxd3 is impossible, unlike Qd1+/Qd2+ which simply drop the queen. After Qd3+ the white king is confined to b1/b2/c1 while I walk my king up to deliver mate, and there is no stalemate since three squares remain.

I'm down to a bare king against queen and king, so both moves lose; I just need to pick the one that drags things out. Kc1 lets Black play Qd2+ immediately driving me to the b-file edge, so Kb2 keeps my king off the back rank a moment longer.

This is a basic king-and-queen mate; I want to shrink White's king box without allowing stalemate. Qc3+ is check and confines the king to just a2 and b1, after which I can walk my king up to deliver mate.

moves.thought: Black's queen on c3 sits right next to my king and the black king on e4 is two files away, so it isn't defended. Kxc3 simply wins the queen and leaves bare kings — an immediate draw instead of a lost position.

new_lessons: [endgame] With queen versus lone king, never put the queen on a square touching that king unless your own king guards it; test Kxq before every check Example: 66...Qc3+? Kxc3 threw away a won K+Q vs K and drew

[middlegame] Before any move, list every enemy unit that can capture the destination square — pawn, piece, or king — and only play it if the recapture count favours you Example: ...Qc3 forked rooks but bxc3 took the queen; Ng5 died to hxg5

[opening] When an enemy pawn wedges into your camp on the 6th/7th rank, capture or blockade it immediately; piece trades that leave it alive cost a piece later Example: 10...Nxd2 ignored the d6 pawn; cxd6 was needed, d6-d7xe7 wrecked my structure

[opening] When your bishop is attacked, choose the retreat that checks or gains a tempo and prevents the opponent's planned central push, not the passive square Example: 6...Bb6 instead of Bb4+ allowed e5, d6 wedge; winning chances fell 50%→32%

[middlegame] Keep a knight or bishop on an advanced central square only if a pawn can support it; otherwise retreat it before pawns or rooks chase it Example: Unsupported Ne4 had no safe squares after e5/d6; Bd5 and Be4 were chased by pawns

[middlegame] Count the whole capture sequence on a square, not defender numbers: two enemy rooks hitting a knight defended by a knight wins two pieces for a rook Example: 26.Ne5: Rxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 gave up two knights for one rook

[middlegame] If your piece is already hit by stacked heavy pieces, trade it or retreat it at once; adding a cheap defender only feeds the exchange sequence Example: 27.Nhf3 "defended" Ne5; Rxe5 Nxe5 Rxe5 collected both knights instead

[middlegame] Never move pawns in front of your king while an enemy bishop or queen eyes those squares; meet a wing pawn storm with a central break or file-opening capture Example: 17.g3 invited fxg3 and Bxh3; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[middlegame] Each move, name your undefended pieces and squares where one enemy move hits two of them; fix the loosest before starting anything active Example: Loose bishop plus loose pawn gave Black free tempi: ...Nb4, ...d5, ...f5

[middlegame] With a material edge play the simplest consolidating move and trade pieces, not pawns; refuse knight tours that leave pieces loose Example: A piece up, Be4 instead of Nc3 threw away most of the advantage

[middlegame] Never give queen for rook or less voluntarily, and guard enemy entry squares (c2, d3, g4, your sixth rank) with pawn or piece before invaders arrive Example: ...Qc3 bxc3 turned a crushing attack into a lost grind; rook reached d6-c6 freely

[endgame] Keep extra pawns connected and mutually defended; pick the recapture that keeps the chain linked even if it doubles a pawn Example: 29...dxc4 scattered a6/c4/c6 and Rd6-b6-a6 ate them; bxc4 held everything

[endgame] Before your king grabs material, count the pawn race and confirm your king stays inside the square of every enemy passer Example: 44...Kxh4 won a rook but f4-f5-f6 and the h-pawn made two queens

[endgame] Before simplifying, name the exact ending you enter and confirm it is a known win; bishop or pawns versus rook is usually only a draw Example: Trading into rook-versus-bishop after Qc3 was objectively lost despite "extra pawns"
